extra.message: pickle.loads() is called on user-controlled input from request.body and request.GET (lines 70-74). An attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload to achieve arbitrary code execution on the server.

eval() is called on user-controlled input from request.GET.get('expr') (line 90). The builtins are stripped but a sufficiently determined attacker may still find a way to execute arbitrary Python code.

cwe: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Eval')

extra.message: urllib.request.urlopen() is called with an SSL-verified=False context. Although the endpoint URL is hardcoded to 'https://partner.invalid/status', no parameterized SSRF exists here, but the unverified SSL context could be exploited if the endpoint is ever made configurable.

The filename from request.GET.get('name') is used directly to construct a file path at line 178 without sanitization. An attacker can use '..' sequences in the 'name' parameter to write files outside the intended directory (e.g., name=../../etc/cron.d/malicious).

The 'ref' parameter from request.GET is used directly as a filename at line 82 without path sanitization. Combined with the PII data (SSN, credit card) written to the file at lines 83-84, this allows an attacker to write files outside the intended directory via '..' traversal.

Jinja2 Template is constructed from user-controlled input (request.GET.get('fragment')) at line 144 and rendered without using a sandboxed environment. An attacker can craft a Jinja2 template expression to read files, execute commands via os.system, or achieve RCE through {{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }} attacks.

cwe: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Template Injection')

extra.message: The 'lane' GET parameter is used directly as the redirect target at line 49 without validation. An attacker can craft a URL like /ops/after/payroll-wayback-card-105/?lane=https://evil.com to phish users on a fake login page.

All operations endpoints (lines 28-197) are exposed without CSRF protection. Despite the INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN gate, these sensitive operations (data import, binary upload, deserialization) are unprotected against CSRF for any legitimate requests coming from authenticated browsers.

At line 170-171, payload.get('filter') (user-controlled JSON input) is passed directly to MongoClient.find_one(). An attacker can inject arbitrary NoSQL queries to bypass authentication, enumerate data, or execute server-side code via $where operators.

At lines 128-129, the Origin header (line 126) is reflected into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and credentials are enabled. This allows any attacker-controlled origin to make authenticated cross-origin requests, enabling full credential-based XSS via CORS misconfiguration.

cwe: CWE-942: Open Reliance on Element in Uncontrolled Context

extra.message: At lines 136-137, X-XSS-Protection is set to '0' (disabling browser XSS filter) and Content-Security-Policy is cleared. This actively weakens the browser's built-in security protections for this endpoint.

Lines 33-35 expose internal server details (BASE_EXPORT_DIR path) and the requested parameter value in error responses. Similarly, line 63 leaks balance/limit ledger state and line 96 exposes env variables like DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE.

At line 84, PII data (SSN and credit card number) from GET parameters is written directly to a file without any validation or masking. This creates sensitive data exposure in log files or exported attachments.

At line 310 during CSV import, the password is set to 'changeme123' as a default when not provided in the CSV. This hardcoded weak password means imported users without an explicit password get a trivially guessable credential.
At line 74, the default database password 'hrpayroll123' is embedded in the source code. If environmental variables are not set (development), this weak hardcoded password will be used.

SECRET_KEY at line 10 has a hardcoded default 'django-insecure-local-dev-only-change-in-production'. In production environments where SECRET_KEY env var is not set, attackers who know this default can forge Django sessions and CSRF tokens.

At line 27, API keys are hashed using plain SHA-256 without a salt or work factor. This makes them vulnerable to rainbow table attacks. Django's default make_password uses PBKDF2 with salt which is far more secure.

cwe: CWE-916: Use of One-Way Hash without a Salt

extra.message: At line 68, new_salary is taken directly from request.POST.get('new_salary') and stored without type validation. When passed to CompensationChangeRequest.objects.create(), the string value (e.g., '999999') can be improperly interpreted by Django's DecimalField, potentially allowing arbitrary salary values.

cwe: CWE-602: Developer Error Leading to Injection

extra.message: At lines 91-99, the api_employees endpoint returns email addresses for all employees. When coupled with the sensitive fields in employee_detail (lines 114-122), this creates a data exposure risk as emails are PII that may not need to be exposed via public API.

At line 12, DEBUG defaults to True when the DEBUG env var is not set. In production deployments where environment variables may not be configured, Django debug mode could remain active, exposing full stack traces and sensitive configuration data.

At lines 61-64, the webhook URL from request.POST.get('url') is stored directly without any validation. This enables Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) when webhooks are triggered to arbitrary internal or external URLs.

All API endpoints (lines 80, 103, 125, 146) use @csrf_exempt decorator. They rely on custom auth (_api_auth). While the design intention is to support API key authentication, this also means any session-based request to these endpoints bypasses CSRF protection, and the webhook creation endpoint has no validation of the URL being stored.
